item.title: Cabinet backtracks on box 3 tax plans for small savings
item.description:
Cabinet backtracks on box 3 tax plans for small savings

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet has promised to rewrite part of its new tax plan for savings and investments, just two days after announcing it, so that fewer people with modest savings are impacted.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen, of the right-wing liberal VVD, made the commitment in parliament on Thursday after MPs from both opposition and coalition parties attacked the plan.

“I have discussed this with the prime minister and with the coalition,” the Financieel Dagblad reported him as saying. “We are prepared to make changes. There will be a proposal to spare small savers.”

Under the plan presented on Tuesday, people would pay 36% tax on returns above €1,000 a year from 2028, down from €1,800 in the earlier version of the reform. Heinen also said he still believed the plan would exempt couples with up to €100,000 in savings.

No funding yet
The minister said he did not yet know how the cabinet would make up the shortfall. Small savers were the main source of funding for the box 3 overhaul, which reports say could cost up to €20 billion.

“We don’t have many levers to pull,” Heinen said. “And every choice you make is enormously complicated.”

The cabinet will send the bill to the Council of State, the government’s senior advisory body on legislation, without an alternative source of funding. Heinen said he would come up with proposals by October 12, when MPs debate the cabinet’s annual package of tax changes.

He also said he would look again at a temporary measure for next year, which would cut the tax-free allowance from €59,357 to €30,846 per person and raise the tax rate. You can find out more about how the changes would affect you in our box 3 explainer.

item.title: Dutch royal house earned nearly half a billion from slavery
item.description:
Dutch royal house earned nearly half a billion from slavery

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch royal family, the House of Orange-Nassau, earned an estimated €576 million from slavery, mostly in the former Dutch East Indies, according to a new investigation into the monarchy.

The research was commissioned by king Willem-Alexander, who granted access to the royal archives and funded the inquiry.

“All stadtholders, kings, and queens, at least up to and including Wilhelmina, were convinced of the legitimacy of colonialism and its importance for the Netherlands,” lead researcher Gert Oostindie said during a ceremony on Friday to present the findings.

The 2,000 page report has been published into five books and was presented to the king. Willem-Alexander described the conclusions as “heartbreaking and confronting” during the gathering at the Academy Building in Leiden.

“I cannot change the past, but I can make a positive contribution to the present and the future to the best of my ability,” he said.

According to the research, the royals earned very little from the transatlantic slave trade, not because they were opposed but because they were unsuccessful.

Oostindie’s work found that while monarchs voiced support for the institution, few had a direct impact on policy.

Only King William I, who was in power from 1813 to 1840, had a direct hand in colonial slavery. Prior to that, leaders left it to the States General, the country’s early administrative assembly, or to the powerful Dutch East India Company (VOC).

After the reign of William I, monarchs were forced to share power with an increasingly important parliament, which made most of the policy decisions.

Willem-Alexander asked Oostindie, a former professor of colonial history, to conduct the investigation in 2022. Sixty researchers were involved in the nearly four year project.

In 2023, the king formally apologised for the Netherlands’ slave trading history during an annual commemoration for the abolition of the practice.

The monarch also stopped using a ceremonial golden coach which has repeatedly come under fire for a painted panel that depicts scenes of colonialism.

Research by the home affairs ministry in 2023 came to a similar conclusion. That study, carried out following a 2021 parliamentary motion, involved some 30 academics and historians and was published as the book Staat en slavernij (State and slavery).

item.title: Rivers too low for depth checks, leaving ships to risk stranding
item.description:
Rivers too low for depth checks, leaving ships to risk stranding

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Rivers in the east of the Netherlands have fallen so low that the authorities can no longer measure whether ships can pass safely, leaving skippers to decide for themselves whether or not to sail and risk getting stranded.

Rijkswaterstaat, the transport ministry department that manages the waterways, told broadcaster NOS its survey boats can no longer reach the shallowest stretches of the IJssel, the Nederrijn, the Pannerdensch Kanaal and much of the Waal.

In certain places the channel is less than 125cm deep, leaving only three agency boats that are shallow enough, but they are also needed in other regions.

Without them, Rijkswaterstaat cannot publish its daily shipping readings of the depths, which barge operators use to avoid getting stranded. Commercial firms collect and sell similar data, but not every skipper has or can pay for a subscription.

Transport under pressure
“This is very worrying,” Fiona Oomen, of inland shipping association Koninklijke Binnenvaart Nederland, told NOS. “All transport is under pressure, on the roads and on the waterways. What if the water drops even further? Where is everything supposed to go?”

The flow of the Rhine at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands, is now around 545 cubic metres per second. That is well below the record low of 614 set in August.

Last weekend a Dutch cruise ship carrying 140 passengers became stuck at Cologne as the Rhine dropped to new lows in Germany.

On the IJssel, a one-way system imposed last week has forced some vessels to take a detour of up to 300km.

Freight carried on Dutch waterways fell by 19% in August, according to CBS figures, with cross-border traffic with Germany worst hit.

The infrastructure ministry lifted the national water shortage in early September, but warned that river levels could stay low until the end of the year. The cabinet has ruled out compensation for businesses hit by the drought.

Rain needed
Rijkswaterstaat could not say how long the situation would last. “We need rain in the catchment area,” a spokesman told NOS, adding that it would have to fall mainly outside the Netherlands. Current forecasts suggest the flow will not get worse, but will not improve much either.

He warned that a different problem would follow. “When it’s over, we get the next problem,” he said. “Then we’ll have high water again.” The North Sea is currently exceptionally warm, which could mean a very wet autumn.

item.title: Inflation rate rose slightly in August
item.description:
Inflation rate rose slightly in August

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

New numbers from the Dutch statistics agency CBS show  the inflation rate rose slightly in August.

The preliminary estimate from the Central Agency for Statistics shows a 0.1% rise from August, putting September’s inflation rate at 3.4%.

The final numbers will be released on October 13.

Fuel and energy prices account for most of the increase. The cost of petrol and gas for heating is was up 13.9% in September over the same month the year before.

Grocery prices, however, have dropped slightly for the second month in a row. Food staples were down 1.3% over the year before, after dropping 0.5% in August.

item.title: The Netherlands had its first TV broadcast 75 years ago
item.description:
The Netherlands had its first TV broadcast 75 years ago

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Seventy-five years ago today, the Dutch had their first opportunity to watch a television broadcast: a performance of the play De Toverspiegel, live from a studio in Bussum.

The Royal Family watched the 90-minute production from the Soestdijk Palace.

Concerns about television’s corrupting influence on society and a focus on post-war reconstruction meant that the Netherlands entered the television era only in 1951, later than the United Kingdom or the United States.

The BBC had begun broadcasting in 1936.

The country had around 500 television sets at the time. Radio was the much more widely consumed medium, with around 250,000 devices in homes across the Netherlands.

A television set cost 785 guilders, about a third of the average annual salary, putting the luxury good far out of reach for most of the country.

Media historian Huub Wijfjes told the NOS that initial television broadcasts simply copied whatever was on the radio. “TV took a dominant position and reached its peak in the 60s, 70s, and 80s. The medium displaced radio,” he said.

By 1956, there were 75,000 television sets in the country.

On the website for the Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision, you can watch the early broadcasts.

item.title: Israeli group disrupts Delft screening of Gaza documentary Naza
item.description:
Israeli group disrupts Delft screening of Gaza documentary Naza

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A premiere screening of the documentary Naza, which investigates the killing of civilians by the Israeli military in Gaza, was interrupted in a Delft cinema on Thursday afternoon by a woman taking a microphone and addressing the audience about the October 7 massacres.

She stood in front of the screen midway through the film and began describing how her family members were murdered during the Hamas attacks that sparked the Gaza war in 2023.

The crowd booed her off stage, the microphone was disabled, some shouted “shame on you”, though some applauded her. The woman’s name is Sabine Taasa, a French-Israeli citizen from a town near the Gaza strip and who lost her husband and a son during the attacks.

An Israeli activist group Ad Kan accompanied Taasa to the screening. The group describes itself as former army and intelligence officers who infiltrate and obstruct what they say are anti-Israeli and anti-Semitic activities in foreign countries.

Another member tried to project footage from the October 7 attacks in the cinema while Taasa spoke, according to broadcaster NOS.

Naza, which has been lauded by critics, consists of anonymous interviews with 24 members of Israeli intelligence and military services. They describe how they attacked Gaza, how AI systems were used to select targets, and the policies toward collateral damage and loss of innocent life.

Some describe killing hundreds of civilians at a time to target single military figures; others describe using surveillance techniques to wait for militants to be at home with their families before striking – a tactic known as “where’s daddy”.

Israeli officials have condemned the film, with prime minister Netanyahu pledging to strip the film makers of their citizenship. Other military figures have disputed the claims made in the film and branded it propaganda.

Dutch-Israeli relations have been strained recently over the decision to ban imports of goods from illegal settlements in occupied Palestinian territories. Dutch diplomats have had their status stripped in response.

item.title: Late goal earns Oranje 2-2 draw with Greece

Late goal earns Oranje 2-2 draw with Greece

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands avoided a first defeat under head coach Xavi Hernandez on Thursday night, coming back from 2-0 down to draw 2-2 with Greece in the Nations League.

Substitute Tijjani Reijnders scored the equaliser from close range in the 89th minute in Thessaloniki.

Greece, who had already won away against Serbia and Germany, made it 2-0 on the stroke of half-time.

Xavi brought on Noa Lang, Ryan Gravenberch and Reijnders at the break for Van Bommel, Guus Til and Quinten Timber.

Captain Virgil van Dijk headed in a goal from the corner at 59 minutes in.
Denzel Dumfries twice had the ball in the net, but both goals were ruled out for offside.

Reijnders then scored the equaliser in the 89th minute. The Netherlands has now conceded in 11 consecutive matches, their longest run since a 16-game streak between 1956 and 1958.

“The way it went in the first half was unacceptable,” Van Dijk told broadcaster NOS. “We were outplayed before the break and that simply can’t happen. We showed a lot of good things in the second half, but that has to be there from the start.”

Oranje opened the campaign with a 1-1 draw against Germany in Amsterdam before beating Serbia in Belgrade. The draw leaves them on 5 points from 3 games, 2 behind Greece.

item.title: Real estate agents to face mandatory register as self-regulation
item.description:
Real estate agents to face mandatory register as self-regulation

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The government plans to introduce a register of real estate agents as well as a complaints desk for buyers and sellers after an investigation revealed widespread dissatisfaction with the industry.

In a letter to parliament on Thursday, housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan said the moves come after attempts to get the sector to regulate itself had failed.

“Unfortunately, I must conclude that the professional associations are unable to take the necessary further steps,” the D66 minister wrote.

Until 2001, real estate agents had to be licensed, like lawyers and architects. Currently, anyone can call themselves a real estate agent and while there are two trade organisations in the Netherlands, both say they don’t have the ability to stand up to unscrupulous agents.

“We have consistently said over the past few years that a voluntary approach does not work here. The minister is now drawing the same conclusion,” Tristan Bons, deputy director of real estate association Vastgoed Nederland said in a statement.

According to Bons, the association doesn’t have the power to punish anyone as membership is voluntary and problem agents can simply leave the group.

Nearly a third of the respondents to the government-commissioned survey had at least one negative experience with a real estate agent. Almost 90% of those complaints involved an agent affiliated with a trade association.

Just 2% of people made an official complaint. Complaints vary from passing along confidential information to driving up the price of housing.

In August, homeowners association Vereniging Eigen Huis said it had received 900 reports between February and July on a special hotline for issues with real estate agents. Issues ranged from buyers feeling pressure to bid beyond their budgets to agents favouring certain clients over others.

item.title: Dutch museum visits rose to over 30m last year
item.description:
Dutch museum visits rose to over 30m last year

October 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More than 30 million people visited a museum in the Netherlands in 2025, a 2.5% increase over the year prior, according to trade association Museumvereniging.

Dutch museums welcomed 31.6 million visitors in 2025, almost back to pre-pandemic levels. In 2019, museums saw 32.6 million guests.

Nearly 90% of Dutch people go to a museum at least once a year, the Museumcijfers 2025 report found.

In 2025 the Netherlands had 492 registered museums. Most institutions are history museums, making up 62%, followed by art museums, which account for 24%.

The use of the yearly Museum Card hit a record high of 9.7 million visits in 2025. Visits using the subscription service is up 5% over the 2019 peak.

A recent survey by Ipsos I&O found that trust in museums is high and most adults consider them to be an important part of society.
